name: Arc (Arc Gateway)
baseline: nginx (C) as an HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 reverse proxy; version, build and the configuration behind the README table are not stated (the repo's benchmark script uses worker_processes auto and upstream keepalive 1024)
workload: Reverse-proxy throughput measured with wrk at 256 and 512 concurrent connections on WSL2 Debian with 2 vCPU, plus an HTTP/2 high-concurrency success rate and the proxy latency overhead.
claimed_speedup: README Performance table: HTTP/1.1 proxy c=256 102,203 RPS vs nginx 49,930 RPS (2.05x); c=512 96,143 vs 41,740 RPS (2.30x); HTTP/2 high concurrency 100% success vs 91.5% for nginx; proxy latency overhead +0.82 ms vs +1.35 ms (39% lower).
compiler_and_flags: Arc built with cargo build --release -p arc-gateway (docs/benchmarks/index.mdx); nginx build and flags not stated; wrk and h2load used as load generators
hardware: WSL2 Debian, 2 vCPU (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Linux io_uring only (the docs recommend kernel 6.1 or newer; no macOS); very young project (11 commits at the time of reading) that the README marks as in active testing; thread-per-core design; feature set (rate limiting, XDP/eBPF DDoS protection) goes beyond a plain proxy.
caveats: First-party numbers; the README table gives no nginx version or configuration, no CPU model and no tool flags. The repo ships a reproducible benchmark workflow (benchmark/scripts/run_h1_wrk_vs_nginx.sh, which writes the nginx.conf it uses and records versions in env.txt) but benchmark/results holds only .gitkeep, so no raw runs are published. In that script the backend is a Python http.server ThreadingHTTPServer returning 2 bytes, Arc runs with ARC_WORKERS=1 by default while nginx uses worker_processes auto, and wrk runs on the same 2 vCPU host as the servers; a Python backend is unlikely to sustain the 50k to 100k RPS in the table, so the backend behind the README numbers is probably different and is not stated. The HTTP/2 row compares success rates, not speed. The docs benchmark page at arc.sdjz.wiki was not opened. Tier C: first-party with partial methodology.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/nginx-alternative (3 repos) and github.com/topics/web-server?l=rust; README, benchmark/README.md, docs/benchmarks/index.mdx and benchmark/scripts/run_h1_wrk_vs_nginx.sh opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: The README attributes it to a thread-per-core architecture on Linux io_uring with lock-free algorithms; no profile or ablation is given.

name: Traefik (Go reverse proxy; TLS latency vs Nginx and HAProxy)
baseline: Nginx 1.28.3 (C) and HAProxy 3.3.6 (C) in Docker; proxy configs live in configs/{nginx,caddy,traefik,haproxy}/ and were not displayed
workload: Fixed-rate load of 5,000 req/s for 20 s with Vegeta (64 connections, about 20 KB JSON payload, 5 s warmup, shuffled order) through each proxy to a backend, over plain HTTP/1.1, HTTPS/1.1 and HTTPS/2.
claimed_speedup: README results (approximate values, all four at 100% success): HTTPS/1.1 Traefik mean about 0.48 ms and P99 about 1.47 ms, Nginx P99 about 24 ms; HTTPS/2 Traefik mean about 0.46 ms and P99 about 1.37 ms, HAProxy P99 about 1.79 ms. Plain HTTP/1.1: all four within about 5%, Caddy and HAProxy lowest mean (about 0.41 ms), HAProxy lowest P99 (about 1.09 ms). Per-proxy tables for every scenario are not published.
compiler_and_flags: Official container images: Nginx 1.28.3, Caddy 2.11.2, Traefik 3.6.13, HAProxy 3.3.6; Vegeta v12.13.0; no compiler flags (prebuilt images)
hardware: Not stated (Docker on the author's machine; an optional restricted run limits each proxy to 2 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM)
tradeoffs: The benchmark records latency percentiles and success rate only; CPU and memory use are not reported. The author states that Nginx wins plaintext throughput and recommends running the suite on one's own hardware.
caveats: Benchmark repo is a third-party suite but a 0-star personal repo that the owner archived on 2026-07-17, with no hardware stated and only approximate best-per-scenario values in the README. It is a fixed-rate latency test at 5,000 req/s, not a saturation throughput test. The Nginx TLS P99 of about 24 ms probably reflects configuration (session cache, buffer sizes) rather than the language gap, and the configs were not read; the README itself says 'in this environment'. No HTTP/1.1 win: the author calls plain HTTP 'extremely tight' and credits Nginx with plaintext throughput. Tier C: partial methodology, hardware missing.

name: Go net/http vs nginx on localhost (yosssi gist)
baseline: nginx (C); version and configuration not shown
workload: wrk -t12 -c400 -d2s against 127.0.0.1 for nginx and for Go net/http servers (empty handler, 'Hello' handler and three static-file variants).
claimed_speedup: nginx 31,780.82 req/s (avg latency 7.71 ms); Go empty handler with GOMAXPROCS=2 62,314.54 req/s (3.79 ms), about 1.96x (derived from page data); Go file server that copies with io.Copy 59,517.07 req/s (5.01 ms), about 1.87x (derived from page data). Other Go file-serving variants are slower than nginx: http.FileServer 16,088.43 req/s and http.ServeContent 25,581.43 req/s.
tradeoffs: Go runtime and GC; no TLS, keep-alive tuning or real file workload is exercised.
caveats: Weak, informal result. Runs last only 2 seconds, the load generator and servers share one machine (the author's home-directory paths and a 'mac:~' prompt in the gist suggest macOS), and Go and nginx versions, nginx configuration and the served content are not given. Every run shows socket errors (connect 155, timeouts 66). The empty-handler and Hello rows do not serve files, so they are not like-for-like with nginx; only the file-server rows are, and two of the three are slower than nginx. Two of the Go sections show identical code and one comment points out they look identical. Gist has no licence, so the code is reference only. Tier C: numbers without methodology.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): '"faster than nginx" OR "outperforms nginx" ... requests/sec README' surfaced the gist 'Go networking performance vs Nginx'; gist opened with WebFetch

name: TrueAsync Server (PHP extension with a C core, HttpArena true-async-server entry)
language: C (PHP extension; HttpArena labels the entry PHP)
baseline: nginx (C, custom handler module compiled -O3 -march=native, per HttpArena frameworks.json); Drogon (C++, CMake Release build), h2o (C), agensio and proxygen (C++) rows from the same suite
workload: HttpArena baseline-h2c, baseline-h2 (TLS) and static-h2 profiles (HTTP/2 over cleartext and TLS, 256 to 4096 connections) and the HTTP/1.1 baseline-4096 profile on one 64-core machine; the server is a PHP extension that runs HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 on a libuv coroutine loop with a trivial PHP handler.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the project; ratios derived from HttpArena result JSON (derived from page data). baseline-h2c: 6,038,026 vs nginx 2,456,329 req/s at 256 connections (2.46x), 3,991,541 vs 2,490,271 at 1024 (1.60x), 3,753,829 vs 2,519,351 at 4096 (1.49x). baseline-h2 (TLS): 4,969,431 vs 3,414,750 at 256 (1.46x), 3,288,741 vs 3,320,285 at 1024 (0.99x). static-h2 at 256: 1,035,118 vs 802,090 (1.29x). baseline-4096 (HTTP/1.1): 2,260,254 vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.12x) but below nginx 3,284,513 (0.69x).
compiler_and_flags: Pre-built image trueasync/php-true-async:0.7.0-rc.6-php8.6 (PHP 8.6 TrueAsync fork) with opcache.jit=1255; the extension's own build flags are not visible in the benchmark Dockerfile; nginx -O3 -march=native; Drogon CMake Release with jemalloc preloaded
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX 64-Cores (128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22 (HttpArena site/data/current.json)
stars_or_usage: 72 stars; listed in HttpArena as an emerging, tuned-mode entry
tradeoffs: Needs the TrueAsync fork of PHP 8.6, libnghttp2 1.57 or newer and OpenSSL 3.0 (3.5 for HTTP/3); handlers are PHP callbacks, static files are served from C.
caveats: Beats nginx only on the HTTP/2 baseline profiles at low connection counts and on static-h2; it loses to nginx on baseline-4096 (0.69x), pipelined (0.57x), limited-conn (0.68x), json-h2c (about 0.71x) and json-tls (0.60x), and it trails the C++ agensio (14,744,015 req/s at baseline-h2-256) and C h2o (16,106,978) by roughly 3x on HTTP/2. Response sizes differ: bytes per response derived from the bandwidth column are about 21 for TrueAsync versus about 62 (h2c) and 87 (h2) for nginx, so part of the gap is header bytes. The HttpArena nginx entry is a custom handler module, not stock nginx. Extension build flags are not shown, so the tier stays at B. The core is C code (llhttp, nghttp2, libuv), so this is a C library with a PHP front end rather than a PHP-versus-C result; the repo itself publishes no benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: raw.githubusercontent.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena site/data/results/*.json and frameworks.json (all result files compared against nginx.json, h2o.json, drogon.json, agensio.json); github.com/true-async/server and its commits page opened; HttpArena frameworks/true-async-server Dockerfile, meta.json and README read
why_faster: The HttpArena README for the entry credits one OS thread and libuv event loop per CPU with SO_REUSEPORT, llhttp and nghttp2 in C, and static files served from C without entering PHP.
